title: Trustworthy, near-instant insurance settlement at negligible per-claim cost

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a broadly reliable way to verify and settle small individual insurance claims almost immediately, with settlement costs low enough to be negligible in the economics of the policy. It would establish that a covered loss occurred, determine its amount under the contract and deliver the appropriate payment while controlling missed losses, erroneous payments and manipulation. Individual loss verification is a central difficulty: its cost can make insurance uneconomical when coverage amounts are small.

Parametric insurance provides an existing route to faster payment by using a predefined event measure, such as a physical disaster parameter, instead of assessing each insured person's loss. That creates basis risk: an insured person can suffer a loss without receiving an adequate payment, or receive a payment without a corresponding loss. The proposed capability would combine inexpensive settlement with trustworthy protection against individual covered losses across diverse small claims. Improving an index can help, but does not itself establish that capability.

Scope synthesis: This is a combined advance in loss measurement, contract design, incentive controls, privacy and settlement operations. It would need to work for people with incomplete records or poor connectivity, and provide an accessible route to challenge mistakes. Near-instant settlement and negligible cost are proposed objectives whose operational definitions remain to be agreed; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate their general achievement.

significance.text: If demonstrated broadly, this capability could expand the practical reach of indemnity insurance by removing a documented obstacle to small policies: individual verification can cost too much relative to the coverage provided. Reducing that cost while preserving meaningful protection would make some previously uneconomical policies more feasible. The supplied research supports this mechanism, but does not quantify administration as a share of premiums or establish the size of the resulting market.

Conditional downstream synthesis: Prompt payment could give households or small businesses funds while recovery decisions are still being made, potentially helping them repair assets, maintain essential spending or avoid disruptive coping measures. Those benefits would depend on adequate coverage, reliable delivery and payment arriving when it is useful. The supplied sources do not demonstrate these recovery effects for the proposed system.

Impact limits synthesis: Lower settlement costs would reduce one component of insurance expense; expected insured losses would still have to be financed. Pricing, capital, distribution, consumer trust and any necessary subsidies would continue to affect affordability and adoption. The revolutionary claim therefore concerns a broadly validated ability to combine speed, low cost and accurate individual protection. Faster payment processing alone, or better index zoning in one setting, would represent a narrower advance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability within this proposal is obtaining credible evidence of individual covered losses and their value at very low cost, without sacrificing protection. Conventional verification can be expensive, while index-based settlement substitutes an observable proxy for the actual loss. Errors in that proxy can produce both missed-loss payments and payments without corresponding losses. The NBER paper emphasizes that failures to pay after damaging losses can be particularly costly to insured households.

Engineering synthesis: A general solution would need to establish coverage, distinguish genuine damage from misleading evidence, value losses consistently and handle uncertain or conflicting information. It would also need to resist manipulation without making verification so burdensome that the speed and cost advantages disappear. Contract terms and incentives must work together: making payment easy to obtain can change behavior, while overly restrictive controls can exclude legitimate claims. The supplied paper documents the relevance of moral hazard; the broader implementation requirements here are proposed deductions from the capability's scope.

Engineering synthesis: Privacy, sparse records, unreliable connectivity and unusual losses create additional barriers to generality. A system must determine when automated evidence is sufficient and when a claim needs further review, then account for the resulting delay and expense. Appeals and difficult cases cannot simply be excluded from performance reporting. Establishing accurate reference judgments is itself challenging when losses are disputed or cannot be measured precisely; uncertainty in those judgments must remain visible.

current_state.text: The World Bank Treasury's Disaster Risk Transfer product note, updated in May 2026, describes sovereign parametric insurance that pays according to physical event parameters rather than detailed assessments of actual losses. It states that the relevant parameters are available within weeks of an event. This demonstrates an established mechanism for relatively fast sovereign payouts without individual loss assessment. It does not demonstrate near-instant household claim settlement or accurate individual indemnification.

Enrique Estefania-Salazar, Michael R. Carter, Eva Iglesias and Álvaro Escribano's June 2024 NBER Working Paper 32618, Breaking Boundaries: Lower Tail Dependence Can Triple the Economic Value of Index Insurance for Rural Households, examines redesigning index-insurance zones in northern Kenya. According to the supplied review of its methods and textual results, the analysis estimates roughly a 60% improvement in its insurance-benefit metric at one reference trigger and approximately a tripling at another. These are counterfactual, community-level expected-utility results. They do not represent demonstrated increases in household income, observed settlement improvements or a general system for valuing individual losses.

The working paper's limitations matter to interpretation. Community aggregation can overstate the benefits experienced by individual households, and scarce observations of catastrophic events constrain estimates for the rare losses that insurance is especially intended to address. Its numerical gains therefore support a context-specific modeled opportunity to improve index design. They should not be transferred directly to other populations, hazards or individual indemnity products. The supplied material identifies it as a working paper and does not establish subsequent peer-reviewed publication or independent replication.

The supplied review reports readable access to both the NBER landing page and the full paper, superseding the earlier research pass's access limitation for interpreting this record. The landing page supplies bibliographic information and an abstract; the full paper supplies the methodological context and qualifications. The review also reports a complete World Bank product note. Its conclusions rely on textual evidence rather than inspection of figures or diagrams.

Evidence-bound synthesis: Neither supplied source demonstrates general, independently validated, low-cost individual indemnification at the speed and cost envisioned here. The supplied freshness search record is empty, so the availability of such a system as of November 2026 remains unresolved. This evidentiary boundary does not establish that no such system exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Before evaluation, define contract- and population-specific targets for near-instant payment, negligible per-claim settlement cost and acceptable errors. Specify when the payment-time clock starts, what constitutes completed payment and how additional verification, appeals and failed delivery are counted. Report complete costs per policy and claim, including the allocation of setup and operating expenses. A relative improvement alone would not establish the title's stronger timing and cost objectives. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Predefined payment-time, settlement-cost and error targets with complete cost accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Operate at meaningful scale across several countries, hazards and small-claim types, using independently audited reference assessments with their own uncertainty documented. Publish payment-time distributions, loss-valuation errors, erroneous payments and false denials, especially after severe losses. Report results for people with poor connectivity or incomplete records, and include accessible appeals, adversarial testing and evaluation of privacy intrusion. Error tolerances should be agreed for each contract and population rather than assumed to have a universal numerical threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Independently audited settlement performance across countries, hazards and small-claim types

completion_criteria.text: Proposed comparison and reproducibility criteria: Compare the system with established indemnity and index alternatives under comparable coverage and loss conditions. Demonstrate viable small policies and a substantial combined improvement in cost, speed and accuracy, with independent replication across different operators or settings. Provide enough methodological detail for auditors to assess results while protecting claimant privacy. Report exceptional cases requiring slower review, the resources those cases consume and the conditions under which performance deteriorates. Finite evaluations would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated cost, speed and accuracy gains over comparable insurance alternatives

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — ACT-01, Reliable actuarial measurement of unprecedented catastrophe losses: Better catastrophe measurement could improve event evidence, loss estimation and the design of settlement triggers. ACT-02 focuses on determining and paying individual covered claims accurately, quickly and cheaply. Reliable estimates of catastrophe losses would not by themselves establish each claimant's entitlement or the amount owed.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-03, A scalable actuarial architecture for financing correlated catastrophes: The concepts are complementary. ACT-03 concerns financing many losses that occur together; ACT-02 concerns verifying and settling claims. Efficient settlement would still require sufficient funds to pay claims, while adequate catastrophe financing would still require trustworthy allocation of payments.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-04, Reliable long-horizon mortality and longevity forecasting with honest uncertainty: Mortality and longevity forecasts concern future population outcomes and liabilities. They could inform the pricing and financing of relevant insurance products, whereas ACT-02 concerns the evidence and operations needed to settle a particular covered loss. Shared requirements include honest treatment of uncertainty and independent validation.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-05, Dependable long-horizon economic scenarios for actuarial liabilities: Economic scenarios could help assess future claim costs and the resources available to meet liabilities. ACT-02 addresses settlement of incurred claims. Improvements in long-horizon scenarios would not establish that an individual claim is valid or that it can be settled near-instantly at negligible cost.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-06, Reliable long-term actuarial projection of healthcare costs under structural change: Healthcare cost projection concerns how future costs evolve as conditions change. ACT-02 could overlap with healthcare claims where coverage and payment amounts must be verified, but efficient claim settlement would not resolve uncertainty about long-term healthcare costs. Conversely, accurate cost projections would not eliminate settlement errors.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-07, Accessible lifetime retirement income through transparent, resilient risk pooling: Both concepts seek to make financial protection more accessible and trustworthy. Retirement income pooling centers on lifetime benefit design and resilience; ACT-02 centers on low-cost verification and payment of covered losses. Efficient payment operations may support both, while their actuarial promises and principal risks remain distinct.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not resolve whether a system meeting the proposed capability existed as of November 2026; the freshness search record is empty.
Operational targets for near-instant payment, negligible settlement cost and acceptable errors remain to be defined for particular contracts and populations.

The supplied review does not provide the exact trigger definitions accompanying the approximately 60% and threefold modeled improvements, so those gains remain described at its stated level of specificity.
Independent replication, subsequent publication status and transferability of the NBER working paper's modeled gains are not established by the supplied material.
A practical evaluation must still determine how to obtain credible reference loss assessments, account for their uncertainty and protect claimant privacy.
No supplied review recommendation was rejected; unresolved empirical and operational questions remain qualified rather than treated as resolved.

brief.title: Small insurance claims paid correctly, almost instantly
possible: After a covered loss, a household or small business could receive the right insurance payment almost immediately. Checking what happened and how much is owed would cost so little that even a small claim would be economical to settle.
why: Checking individual losses can cost too much to make small insurance policies worthwhile. Making those checks cheap and reliable could bring meaningful protection to people whose losses are currently uneconomical to insure.
Prompt payments could help households and small businesses repair damage and maintain essential spending while they decide how to recover.

sources.showed: The World Bank provides disaster insurance to governments that pays when physical event measurements meet agreed conditions. Those measurements become available within weeks, avoiding detailed loss assessments.
sources.quote:
WB DRT transactions have all been parametric with 
payouts triggered by the physical parameters of an 
event rather than actual losses incurred.
sources.cited_for: Payments based on event measurements offer an established way to avoid detailed loss assessments.
sources.not_established: Government disaster cover does not establish almost immediate, accurate payment for individual household losses.

sources.who: Enrique Estefania-Salazar, Michael Carter, Eva Iglesias and Álvaro Escribano
sources.showed: An unreviewed working paper modeled better livestock insurance zones in northern Kenya. Grouping areas whose worst losses coincide increased the modeled value of insurance.
sources.quote:
We show that maximizing lower tail dependence is statistically equivalent to minimizing downside
basis risk.
sources.cited_for: Matching areas by how their worst losses coincide can reduce the chance that a damaging loss receives no payment.
sources.not_established: The community-level model does not establish household gains, faster settlement or cheap individual loss checks; independent replication remains absent.

shown: Existing approaches avoid checking every person's loss by paying against a shared measure, such as disaster strength. That can speed payment, but the measure can miss someone's loss or trigger payment when they suffered none.

The Kenya researchers estimated that redrawing insurance zones could roughly triple the modeled benefit under one payment rule. This was a calculation of expected benefits, rather than an observed improvement in household income or claim settlement.
missing: Individual losses and their value still need to be established cheaply enough for small policies, while catching misleading claims.
Speed and cost gains still need to hold when disputed claims, appeals and failed payments are included.
Reliable protection still needs to work with sparse records, poor connectivity and unusual losses while preserving privacy.
Independent trials still need to demonstrate the combined gains across different countries, hazards and kinds of small claim.

milestones.label: Agreed payment, cost and error targets with full accounting
milestones.explanation: An evaluation would have to define timing, cost and error targets beforehand, counting setup, operations, further checks, appeals and failed delivery. This would establish whether payment is almost immediate and settlement costs negligible.

milestones.label: Independently audited results across countries, hazards and small claims
milestones.explanation: Independent audits would have to measure payment times and errors at scale across settings, including severe losses, excluded groups, appeals, manipulation and privacy. This would test whether individual protection remains reliable.

milestones.label: Repeated gains over comparable insurance alternatives
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce combined cost, speed and accuracy gains against comparable insurance alternatives, accounting for slower cases. This would establish viable small policies and the boundaries of performance.

uncertain: How fast is almost immediate, how cheap is negligible, and which errors are acceptable for each contract and population?
How can independent assessors establish a trustworthy comparison when the loss itself is disputed or hard to measure?
Do the modeled benefits of better insurance zones extend to individual households, other places and other hazards?

page.title: Automated indemnity insurance claims settlement
page.definition: A system verifies individual covered losses, calculates the indemnity—the payment owed under the policy—and delivers funds in seconds at costs compatible with low-premium cover. Its performance includes fraud checks, disputed claims, human referrals and failed payments.

goal.need: The Microinsurance Network reports a seven-day median claims turnaround time in its discussion of the 2020 landscape study, and about 35 days for property claims in Latin America and the Caribbean. The article gives no responding sample sizes for these figures. Settlement also retains a measurable cost: Lemonade reports US$14 per pet insurance claim for 2025. These quantities motivate reducing both delay and expense while preserving payment of the contractual benefit.

statements.quote: Lemonade aims for zero paperwork and instant everything.
statements.context: A developer objective stated in its announcement of an insurance product on 27 September 2017.

statements.quote: to handle claims in a timely, fair and transparent manner
statements.context: The application paper invokes Insurance Core Principle 19.10 when discussing claims decisions influenced by artificial intelligence.

completion.title: Independent live replication confirms the combined speed, cost and accuracy of individual indemnification.
completion.criterion: An independent operator reproduces a live indemnity product’s success against externally published limits for payment time, complete settlement cost per claim and individual-loss error. Timing ends when funds become available to the claimant; costs include referrals, disputes and failed payments. The limits must establish payment in seconds and costs compatible with the specified low-premium policy. No numerical joint acceptance limits were located, so this remains a provisional completion test.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no published external completion standard for the combined capability was located.
completion.basis: Searches covered IAIS inclusive-insurance and AI guidance, FCA sandbox criteria, South African microinsurance rules and Lemonade disclosures. They yielded service duties, validation methods and developer results, but no combined numerical test. The fallback joins their speed, fairness and financial-viability objectives. World Bank parametric contracts use event measurements rather than individual losses and therefore do not establish this capability.

milestones.title: An automated claims model withstands stress without compromising accuracy or stability.
milestones.criterion: Under laboratory stress tests involving high workloads, data spikes or sudden changes, an AI claims model maintains accuracy and stability. IAIS section 4.2.1 recommends this outcome alongside testing on previously unseen data and comparison with other models or expected results. It supplies no numerical workload, accuracy tolerance or required sample size; this is a qualitative validation criterion.
milestones.set_by: International Association of Insurance Supervisors, Application Paper on the supervision of artificial intelligence, section 4.2.1; a recommendation for insurance AI generally.
milestones.threshold_quote: Robust systems should handle stress without compromising accuracy or stability.

milestones.title: A microinsurer decides complete claims within 2 business days, with 14 more business days for disputes.
milestones.criterion: In live operations, a microinsurer assesses a claim within 2 business days after receiving all required documents and authorises payment, repudiates the claim, or disputes it and notifies the claimant. For disputed claims, it decides validity and pays or repudiates within 14 business days after the initial period expires. This South African benchmark concerns claim decisions and authorisation; the initial deadline does not require funds to have reached the claimant.
milestones.set_by: South African Financial Sector Conduct Authority, Government Notice 996 of 28 September 2018, rules 2A.9.1–2A.9.2; written for non-life microinsurance.

milestones.title: An insurer approves an individual indemnity claim and sends payment instructions within 3 seconds.
milestones.criterion: From completed claim submission, an automated system checks coverage, screens for fraud, approves the claim and sends payment instructions within 3 seconds. Lemonade reported this for one stolen-coat claim submitted on 23 December 2016; the insured item cost US$979. Its release describes bank instructions, without establishing when funds became available to the claimant. The result is a company report, not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback adopting Lemonade’s published three-second challenge as a component benchmark; no field-wide recognition criterion was located.
milestones.threshold_quote: The number to beat is now 3 seconds, and we hope others will rise to the challenge.

milestones.title: One indemnity product meets externally specified speed, complete-cost and loss-error limits in live use.
milestones.criterion: A live indemnity product jointly meets externally published payment-time, complete per-claim cost and individual-loss error limits, including difficult claims and redress. No qualifying joint protocol or passing result was located. As separate component results, Lemonade reports approximately 55% automated claims as of 31 December 2025 and US$14 per pet claim for 2025. These disclosures provide neither a joint loss-accuracy endpoint nor the claim counts underlying those metrics.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; IAIS product-viability guidance and FCA live-testing criteria do not specify combined acceptance limits for this capability.
